01 / 07 — THE HISTORICAL PROMISE OF FUSION

Crowing Victory

When fusion energy research was first internationally declassified in the 50s, buoyed by the success of controlling nuclear fission, and the simplicity of concepts like the Z-pinch, scientists thought fusion was only a decade away.

However, they were wrong!

Plasma had other ideas — The axisymmetric Z-pinch,

u⃗=uz(r)e^zB⃗=Bθ(r)e^θ\begin{aligned} \vec{u} &= u_{z}(r)\hat{e}_{z} \\ \vec{B} &= B_{\theta}(r)\hat{e}_{\theta} \end{aligned}uB​=uz​(r)e^z​=Bθ​(r)e^θ​​

may have been one of the simplest possible magnetic confinement fusion configurations (MCF) that promised an economical approach to the task without needing applied magnetic fields, but it was prey to virulent fundamental magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modes that limited lifetimes to nanoseconds (ns) — too short for fusion to create net power.

Why did it fail? →

1 / 3

02 / 07 — THE PHYSICAL PROBLEM

The Z-pinch is unstable.

Being a simple axial MHD equilibrium with a self-generated magnetic field is simple, but does not guarantee stability. Two azimuthal modes exist that lead to positive feedback loops which cause the pinch to collapse when perturbed by them.

The Sausage and Kink modes

Two Positive Feedback Loops — When studying plasma instabilities in the Z-pinch we consider perturbations to the plasma displacement whose azimuthal, θ\thetaθ, and axial, zzz components are described by a plane-wave,

ξ∝exp⁡(i(mθ+kz−ωt))\xi \propto \exp\bigg(i (m \theta + k z - \omega t)\bigg)ξ∝exp(i(mθ+kz−ωt))

The sausage mode, m=0m = 0m=0, and kink mode, m=1m = 1m=1, are the two primary instabilities that plague the Z-pinch. Ways to stabilize the system against this either require means that are incompatible with a fusion reactor, e.g., wall-stabilization, or introduce externally applied magnetic fields and do away with the main advantage of the Z-pinch: it generates its own confinement.

What about natural means? →

03 / 07 — Shear-flow stabilization and Kadomtsev Stability

Natural ways to stabilize the Z-pinch

Sheared axial flow, and a logarithmically tailored plasma pressure profile, change the dynamics of perturbations and provide a route toward stabilizing Z-pinch configurations against both the sausage and kink modes.

Scientific Miracles

At the frontier — Work on Z-pinch stabilization in the 60s experienced a major breakthrough when the Russian scientist B.B. Kadomtsev determined that a plasma pressure profile which satisfied the inequality,

−dln⁡(p)dln⁡(r)≤4γ2+γββ=⟨p⟩B22μ0\begin{aligned} -\frac{d{\ln(p)}}{{d\ln(r)}} &\leq \frac{4\gamma}{2 + \gamma \beta} \\ \beta &= \frac{\langle p \rangle }{B^{2}}2\mu_{0} \end{aligned}−dln(r)dln(p)​β​≤2+γβ4γ​=B2⟨p⟩​2μ0​​

will provide stabilization to an unsheared Z-pinch against the m=0m = 0m=0 mode. However, this did not address the kink mode, and in the late 70s, and early 80s, fusion energy researchers began to transition away from pinches, and towards toroidal systems that connected the ends of the pinch together to eliminate end losses and create systems that external magnetic fields could confine.

It wasn’t until the mid-90s when two American researchers found a natural way to stabilize the m=1m = 1m=1 mode using sheared-flow of a sufficient magnitude. By dividing the axial shear by the Alfvenic shear the linearized equations of MHD could be solved numerically to determine how much shear was required for this stabilization. The result is the Shumlak-Hartman criterion,

duzdr>0.1kVAk=2πLVA=Bρμ0\begin{aligned} \frac{d u_{z}}{dr} &> 0.1 kV_{A} \\ k &= \frac{2\pi}{L} \\ V_{A} &= \frac{B}{\sqrt{\rho\mu_{0}}} \end{aligned}drduz​​kVA​​>0.1kVA​=L2π​=ρμ0​​B​​

A Cosmic Joke

The universe has a sense of humor, because to find physics that provides the Z-pinch stability against the interchange, $m = 0$, mode you have to first exchange one around

Willard H. Bennett and the Bennett Pinch

Another godfather of plasma physics — The American scientist Willard H. Bennett worked out the electrostatic theory of magnetically self-focusing streams in 1934 where he used an approximate, self-similar argument to come up with the basis for a non-relativistic number density to describe these systems,

n(r)=n0(1+ξ2r2)2ξ2=CBn0TCB=μ0e2uz,0216kB\begin{aligned} n(r) &= \frac{n_{0}}{(1 + \xi^{2}r^{2})^{2}} \\ \xi^{2} &= \frac{C_{B}n_{0}}{T} \\ C_{B} &= \frac{\mu_{0}e^{2}u_{z,0}^{2}}{16k_{B}} \end{aligned}n(r)ξ2CB​​=(1+ξ2r2)2n0​​=TCB​n0​​=16kB​μ0​e2uz,02​​​

The cubic pureflow Bennett-Shumlak-Hartman-Vortex

If you swap this with the uniform drift flow that he studied you’ll get a new flow profile,

uz(r)=uz,0T(r)2(T(r)+CBn0r2)2u_{z}(r) = u_{z,0}\frac{T(r)^{2}}{(T(r) + C_{B}n_{0}r^{2})^{2}}uz​(r)=uz,0​(T(r)+CB​n0​r2)2T(r)2​

Treating this also as the MHD flow that provides the stabilizing shear, in the ideal limit of an infinitely long plasma cylinder the Shumlak-Hartman criterion relaxes,

uz′>0u_{z}' > 0uz′​>0

and with a power-law temperature profile,

T(r)=TprpnrnT(r) = \frac{T_{p}}{r_{p}^{n}}r^{n}T(r)=rpn​Tp​​rn

it can be shown that n>2n > 2n>2 gives a sufficiently enhanced thermodynamic gradient for this flow to be shear-flow stabilized.

Inserting the minimum thermal energy shear-flow stabilized state, n=3n = 3n=3, leads to

uz(r)=uz0r2(r+C)2u_z(r)=u_{z0}\frac{r^2}{(r+C)^2}uz​(r)=uz0​(r+C)2r2​

which has the shear,

duzdr=2uz0Cr(r+C)3\frac{du_z}{dr}=\frac{2u_{z0}Cr}{(r+C)^3}drduz​​=(r+C)32uz0​Cr​

where

C=μ0e216kBn0uz,02rp3TpC = \frac{\mu_{0}e^{2}}{16k_{B}}\frac{n_{0}u_{z,0}^{2}r_{p}^{3}}{T_{p}}C=16kB​μ0​e2​Tp​n0​uz,02​rp3​​

05 / 07 — The Kadomtsev Connection and Shear-flow stabilization

Shear-flow Stabilization

By linking the drift flow supporting the plasma current density with the center of mass flow a full integrable MHD equilibrium can be determined that is shear-flow stabilized in both ideal and non-ideal senses, as well as Kadomtsev stable

Solving the equilibrium

Stabilization of the Z-pinch hinges upon not just the aforementioned Kadomtsev criterion, but also the Shumlak-Hartman criterion. There is also a non-ideal criterion whose form is approximately rendered here,

duzdr>L2πrpdln⁡(p)dln⁡(r)\frac{du_{z}}{dr} > \frac{L}{2\pi r_{p}}\frac{d\ln(p)}{d\ln(r)}drduz​​>2πrp​L​dln(r)dln(p)​

This approximate version of the non-ideal criterion will not be considered here at the moment.

In order to evaluate the Shumlak-Hartman, and Kadomtsev criteria, we first have to determine the rest of the magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium beyond the uniform density implied by the Bennett exchange procedure, and the cubic pureflow Bennett-Shumlak-Hartman vortex. This means determining the magnetic field, and the plasma pressure by solving some integrals.

The magnetic field for a stationary Z-pinch comes from Ampere’s Law,

Bθ=μ0r∫0rr′Jz(r′)dr′B_{\theta} = \frac{\mu_{0}}{r}\int_{0}^{r}r'J_{z}(r')dr'Bθ​=rμ0​​∫0r​r′Jz​(r′)dr′

and the plasma pressure comes from the force balance,

∇p=J⃗×B⃗=−JzBθ\nabla p = \vec{J}\times\vec{B} = -J_{z}B_{\theta}∇p=J×B=−Jz​Bθ​

with the boundary conditions

p(0)=p0=∫0rpJzBθdrp(rp)=0\begin{aligned} p(0) &= p_{0} = \int_{0}^{r_{p}}J_{z}B_{\theta}dr \\ p(r_{p}) &= 0 \end{aligned}p(0)p(rp​)​=p0​=∫0rp​​Jz​Bθ​dr=0​

If these integrals do not evaluate, or if the magnetic field that we obtain from Ampere’s Law blows up at the origin, then the clever physics we have done is incoherent. However, fortunately that is not the case because the magnetic field can be integrated using u-substituion or a computer algebra system (CAS) like Wolfram Mathematica. In formulating the following equation we have assumed that the plasma current density for a singly-ionized hydrogen-electron plasma,

J⃗=Jze^z=en0uz,0r2(r+C)2e^z\vec{J} = J_{z}\hat{e}_{z} = en_{0}u_{z,0}\frac{r^{2}}{(r + C)^{2}}\hat{e}_{z}J=Jz​e^z​=en0​uz,0​(r+C)2r2​e^z​

depends on the exact same flow profile that we constructed for the center of mass MHD flow,

u⃗=uze^z=uz,0r2(r+C)2e^z\vec{u} = u_{z}\hat{e}_{z} = u_{z,0}\frac{r^{2}}{(r + C)^{2}}\hat{e}_{z}u=uz​e^z​=uz,0​(r+C)2r2​e^z​

This leads to Ampere’s Law being,

Bθ=en0uz,0μ0r∫0rr′3(r′+C)2dr′=en0uz,0μ0f(r,C)2r(r+C)\begin{aligned} B_{\theta} &= \frac{en_{0}u_{z,0}\mu_{0}}{r}\int_{0}^{r}\frac{r'^{3}}{(r' + C)^{2}}dr' \\ &= en_{0}u_{z,0}\mu_{0}\frac{f(r,C)}{2r(r+C)} \end{aligned}Bθ​​=ren0​uz,0​μ0​​∫0r​(r′+C)2r′3​dr′=en0​uz,0​μ0​2r(r+C)f(r,C)​​

where,

f(r,C)=r3−3r2C−6rC2(1+ln⁡(Cr+C))−6C3ln⁡(Cr+C)f(r,C) = r^{3} - 3r^{2}C - 6rC^{2}\bigg(1 + \ln(\frac{C}{r+C})\bigg)-6C^{3}\ln(\frac{C}{r+C})f(r,C)=r3−3r2C−6rC2(1+ln(r+CC​))−6C3ln(r+CC​)

What’s amazing about this function is that it has exactly the properties that we need for our procedure to be valid. Instead of blowing up at the origin we have,

lim⁡r→0+f(r,C)=0\lim_{r\rightarrow 0^{+}} f(r,C) = 0r→0+lim​f(r,C)=0

The Kadomtsev Criterion

The Kadomtsev criterion can be written equivalently as,

ddrln⁡(p⟨jz⟩γ)≤0\frac{d}{dr}\ln\left(\frac{p}{\langle j_z\rangle^\gamma}\right) \leq 0drd​ln(⟨jz​⟩γp​)≤0

where γ\gammaγ is the adiabatic (polytropic) index, and where

⟨jz⟩=1πr2∫jzdA\langle j_{z} \rangle = \frac{1}{\pi r^{2}}\int j_{z}dA ⟨jz​⟩=πr21​∫jz​dA

is area-averaged current density. The derivative here is a doozy, but we can evaluate it,

ddrln⁡(p⟨jz⟩γ)=1FddrF\frac{d}{dr}\ln\left(\frac{p}{\langle j_z\rangle^\gamma}\right) = \frac{1}{F}\frac{d}{dr}Fdrd​ln(⟨jz​⟩γp​)=F1​drd​F

with,

F=p⟨jz⟩γF = \frac{p}{\langle j_{z} \rangle^{\gamma}}F=⟨jz​⟩γp​

so that we have,

1FddrF=1F(dpdr1⟨jz⟩γ−γp⟨jz⟩γ+1ddr⟨jz⟩)\frac{1}{F}\frac{d}{dr}F = \frac{1}{F}\bigg(\frac{dp}{dr}\frac{1}{\langle j_{z} \rangle^{\gamma}} - \gamma \frac{p}{\langle j_{z} \rangle^{\gamma + 1}}\frac{d}{dr}\langle j_{z} \rangle\bigg)F1​drd​F=F1​(drdp​⟨jz​⟩γ1​−γ⟨jz​⟩γ+1p​drd​⟨jz​⟩)

which becomes,

(p′p−γ⟨jz⟩′⟨jz⟩)≤0\bigg(\frac{p'}{p} - \gamma\frac{\langle j_{z} \rangle'}{\langle j_{z} \rangle}\bigg) \leq 0(pp′​−γ⟨jz​⟩⟨jz​⟩′​)≤0

For the equilibrium shown here we can prove that this is satisfied for all physically admissible parameter values of the positive-current pureflow vortex. This follows from the structure of the current density which can be seen to be always positive for any combination of plasma parameters and positive flow speed modulus squared. Then, the same can be said for the magnetic field via Ampere’s Law as integrating this always positive current density will result in a magnetic field that has the same property.

Consequently, p′=−JzBθ<0p' = -J_{z}B_{\theta} < 0p′=−Jz​Bθ​<0 holds throughout the domain for any CCC, and p>0p > 0p>0 does as well because p0>∫0rJzBθdr,∀r s.t. 0<r<rpp_{0} > \int_{0}^{r}J_{z}B_{\theta}dr, \forall r \ s.t. \ 0 < r < r_{p}p0​>∫0r​Jz​Bθ​dr,∀r s.t. 0<r<rp​. Similarly, ⟨jz⟩>0\langle j_{z} \rangle > 0⟨jz​⟩>0 holds likewise, as the integrand is the same as for BθB_{\theta}Bθ​. ⟨jz⟩(r)=2r2G(r),G(r)=∫0rjz(r′)r′dr′ \langle j_{z} \rangle(r) = \frac{2}{r^{2}}G(r), \quad G(r) = \int_{0}^{r}j_{z}(r')r' dr'⟨jz​⟩(r)=r22​G(r),G(r)=∫0r​jz​(r′)r′dr′

⟨jz⟩′=2r(jz−⟨jz⟩) \langle j_{z} \rangle' = \frac{2}{r}\left(j_{z} - \langle j_{z} \rangle \right)⟨jz​⟩′=r2​(jz​−⟨jz​⟩)

jz′(r)=2en0uz,0Cr(r+C)3>0 j_{z}'(r) = 2en_{0}u_{z,0}C \frac{r}{(r + C)^{3}} > 0jz′​(r)=2en0​uz,0​C(r+C)3r​>0

so we have jz(s)<jz(r)j_{z}(s) < j_{z}(r)jz​(s)<jz​(r) for any s<rs < rs<r allowing us to write,

06 / 07 — QUANTITATIVE COMPARISON

What do the experiments show?

Physics needs to meet with experiment to test its validity

Modelling real world systems with an idealized physics

Solving the equilibrium — on real world data requires extending the model to include a non-zero flow at the core of the device. Without it the model treats the problem as rising from stagnation when in reality experimental systems show shear layers that transition between smaller and larger flows / current densities / intensities.

To solve the equilibrium we have to study the boundary conditions,

uz(0)=u0uz(rp)=uedge\begin{aligned} u_{z}(0) &= u_{0} \\ u_{z}(r_{p}) &= u_{edge} \end{aligned}uz​(0)uz​(rp​)​=u0​=uedge​​

The mathematical function we are considering is,

uz(r)=u0±uz,0r2(r+C)2\begin{aligned} u_{z}(r) = u_{0} \pm u_{z,0}\frac{r^{2}}{(r + C)^{2}} \end{aligned}uz​(r)=u0​±uz,0​(r+C)2r2​​

which leads to the following fourth-order algebraic equation when we consider the edge of the plasma / magnetohydrodynamic fluid system,

rp2(uedge−u0∓uz,0)+(uedge−u0)Cuuz,02(Cuuz,02+2rp)=0C=Cuuz,02\begin{aligned} &r_{p}^{2}\bigg(u_{edge} - u_{0} \mp u_{z,0}\bigg) + \\ &\qquad (u_{edge} - u_{0})C_{u}u_{z,0}^{2}\bigg(C_{u}u_{z,0}^{2} + 2r_{p}\bigg) = 0 \\ C &= C_{u}u_{z,0}^{2} \end{aligned}C​rp2​(uedge​−u0​∓uz,0​)+(uedge​−u0​)Cu​uz,02​(Cu​uz,02​+2rp​)=0=Cu​uz,02​​

The roots of this equation are the physical uz,0u_{z,0}uz,0​. They exist because the roots of fourth-order algebraic systems have a closed-form, and we can use existing mathematical libraries like Python’s numpy to obtain them. That is what is done in this section, and the results are presented. The code for producing these results can be found in the caption of the respective figures.

To evaluate the accuracies, two different metrics are used. The first is range-normalized relative root mean square error (RNRRMSE),

RNRRMSE=1max(J^ϕ)−min(J^ϕ)RRMSE(J,J^ϕ)RRMSE=1N∑i=1N(J^i−Ji)2\begin{aligned} RNRRMSE &= \frac{1}{max(\hat{J}_{\phi}) - min(\hat{J}_{\phi})}RRMSE(J, \hat{J}_{\phi}) \\ RRMSE &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{J}_{i} - J_{i})^{2}} \end{aligned}RNRRMSERRMSE​=max(J^ϕ​)−min(J^ϕ​)1​RRMSE(J,J^ϕ​)=N1​i=1∑N​(J^i​−Ji​)2​​

and R2R^{2}R2,

R2=1−SSresSStotSSres=∑i=1N(yi−y^i)2SStot=∑i=1N(yi−yˉ)2\begin{aligned} R^{2} &= 1 - \frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}} \\ SS_{res} &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_{i} - \hat{y}_{i})^{2} \\ SS_{tot} &= \sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2} \end{aligned}R2SSres​SStot​​=1−SStot​SSres​​=i=1∑N​(yi​−y^​i​)2=i=1∑N​(yi​−yˉ​)2​

The former is used to evaluate all of the applications except the laser-driven shock in a water microjet.

Edge Pedestal

The edge pedestal is a confinement barrier that appears in tokamaks, a toroidal magnetic fusion energy concept, in the presence of an enhanced thermodynamic gradient. This equilibrium is both a confinement barrier, and one that appears in the presence of an enhanced thermodynamic gradient. Therefore, despite its cylindrical nature and idealized structure it is a test of the physics to see if it produces accurate solutions to this experimental system.

MAST

Air Plasma Streamer Head

To model the intensity of an air plasma streamer head, a linear discharge model is assumed to relate the observed intensity with the plasma current density,

Iz=αJzI_{z} = \alpha J_{z}Iz​=αJz​

This pits the nonlinear structure of the physics against the nonlinear structure of the experimental observations. If they do not match then this usage of a proportionality constant will not make them.

07 / 07 — THE WORK AHEAD

Towards higher-order study

The analytic understanding of an idealized model for a shear-flow stabilized Z-pinch opens new questions related to the higher-order physics and the stabilizing effect of the shear alongside plasma turbulence. These questions involve investigating eigenmode spectra, nonlinear evolution, nonideal transport, experimental tests, and engineering

Next steps for the research

This is just the beginning — What’s most remarkable about this simplified, idealized model is how well it does at accurately modelling complex experimental systems using their experimental data. That is despite only capturing the effects of ideal magnetohydrodynamics, i.e., only what the plasma would do if it was treated purely as a magnetic spring, and involving a uniform density as well as an enhanced temperature gradient that is a very simplified model of an experimental temperature gradient.

What really needs to happen for this research are two things:

(1) Higher-order theoretical and computational work to analyze resistive physics, kinetic physics, and the effect of instabilities just to name a few. This list is by no means an exhaustive one.

(2) Financial stability for myself. Since graduating with a Master’s of Science in Aeronautics & Astronautics from the University of Washington three years ago it’s been really difficult.

My Story

I spent a year hearing rejection after rejection while I worked on a high-performance 3D+t CUDA C Ideal MHD solver until I finally found a job training AI, and got my code to run equilibrium pinch problems without spazzing out. My function was to come up with novel problems that stumped the AI. On three separate days I managed to do this twelve separate times each day by giving the AI Bennett Pinch problems in the infinitely long plasma cylinder.

Eventually, the people paying me said “you’re doing too much Bennett Pinch. Do something different.” So, I sat down and read Davidson’s Turbulence for three hours but to no avail. Asking an AI problems from a book it’s trained on is not going to work, and it didn’t. With only an hour left on the clock, and a need for the money that came from the stump, I did the only thing I could and that was to swap the Bennett profile around so that I could use my code for solving the Bennett pinch to get a value for the system in the limit, T0>>TpT_{0} >> T_{p}T0​>>Tp​, i.e., treating the temperature as uniform.

I’ve had to carry this research to the point where it’s at by myself. That includes a four month hiatus working for a startup as a 3D Motion Engineer where I built a real-time rendered pipeline in Vulkan and authored an 80 page R&D report which detailed the various tradeoffs and approaches to the digital twin they wanted.

The Present Moment

Right now, I’m at the point where I cannot afford to continue to do this much longer.

I’ve spent the last year, and some change, working on this physics while unemployed, and living with my parents. I love my mom and dad, but it gets old and depressing to be a man in my early 30s, waking up in my parents house for months on end to a jobless existence when you have constructed something profound in physics.

Zap Energy approached me about an opening as a senior scientist around the time that I started posting accurate solutions to their 2001 experimental plasmas from this analytic model, but unfortunately these discussions did not progress beyond an initial negotiation over compensation and equity.

I’m not a greedy or unreasonable person, and I could care less about billions. My ambitions are not centered on accumulating extraordinary wealth. I’m oriented more towards family, financial stability, and having my time free to do research over chasing after monetary excess, and the chain of obligations that come with it. I just wanted to see if they respected the result and myself enough to negotiate with me about this.

Support the Research

The next stage of this research requires resources beyond what an independent researcher can reasonably provide alone.

I am actively seeking:

  • Institutional affiliation and research funding.
  • Collaboration with theoretical, computational, and experimental plasma physicists.
  • Access to experimental facilities, and diagnostic measurements.
  • High-performance computing resources for numerical stability studies.
  • Employment opportunities that would allow this research to continue.

If you are a scientist, research institution, funding organization, or individual interested in advancing this work, I would welcome the opportunity to speak with you. My Linkedin
